questions.topic: Understand the Entity & Design the Audit Strategy
questions.prompt: Assessed risk of material misstatement increases while acceptable audit risk stays constant. What happens to acceptable detection risk?

choices.text: It increases.
It decreases.
It becomes irrelevant.
It must equal control risk.

questions.explanation: More risky assertions require audit procedures that leave a lower risk of failing to detect a material misstatement.

questions.topic: Understand the Entity & Design the Audit Strategy
questions.prompt: A retailer introduces a complex new revenue contract before considering any controls. Which risk is primarily illustrated by the contract’s complexity?

choices.text: Detection risk.
Sampling risk alone.
Inherent risk.
The risk that an audit report is mailed late.

questions.explanation: Inherent risk concerns susceptibility to misstatement before control effects. Complexity may increase that susceptibility.

questions.topic: Understand the Entity & Design the Audit Strategy
questions.prompt: A company experiences falling demand and slow-moving inventory. Which assertion most directly requires additional attention?

choices.text: Cash existence only.
Debt completeness only.
Ownership of the auditor’s workpapers.
Inventory valuation.

questions.explanation: Slow movement and declining demand can indicate inventory is not recoverable at recorded amounts.

questions.topic: Understand the Entity & Design the Audit Strategy
questions.prompt: Illustratively, acceptable audit risk is 4%, inherent risk is 80%, and control risk is 50%. What is planned detection risk?
questions.explanation: Detection risk = .04 ÷ (.80 × .50) = .10. Multiplying all three known inputs does not solve for detection risk.

questions.topic: Understand the Entity & Design the Audit Strategy
questions.prompt: Which planning change primarily changes the nature of evidence?

choices.text: Increasing a sample from 20 to 40 items.
Replacing internal explanations with independent external confirmations.
Moving the same procedure from November to December.
Allowing an extra hour to type the memo.

questions.explanation: Nature concerns the kind of procedure and evidence; sample size is extent and moving the date is timing.

questions.topic: Understand the Entity & Design the Audit Strategy
questions.prompt: Substantive testing reveals a previously unknown side agreement affecting revenue. What should the auditor do?

choices.text: Retain the original assessment to meet the budget.
Assume the agreement cannot affect other transactions.
Reassess risk and revise planned procedures as necessary.
Treat an unmodified prior-year opinion as sufficient evidence.

questions.explanation: Risk assessment is iterative. New evidence may change the audit response and extend testing to similar arrangements.

questions.topic: Understand the Entity & Design the Audit Strategy
questions.prompt: A distributor is entering a new market and implementing a new ERP. Match each issue to the appropriate audit concept or response. Planning observations: Complex warranty estimates require substantial judgment. The new ERP has not implemented approval controls. A lender covenant increases pressure to overstate earnings. The team initially planned interim testing before the ERP conversion. Illustrative risk inputs: For one assertion, acceptable audit risk is 3%, inherent risk is 60%, and control risk is 50%. These percentages are a teaching illustration, not a prescribed audit formula for every engagement. Required: Risk associated with estimate susceptibility before controls.

choices.text: Detection risk
Engagement fee risk
No audit risk
Inherent risk

questions.explanation: Estimate complexity affects inherent susceptibility.

questions.topic: Understand the Entity & Design the Audit Strategy
questions.prompt: A distributor is entering a new market and implementing a new ERP. Match each issue to the appropriate audit concept or response. Planning observations: Complex warranty estimates require substantial judgment. The new ERP has not implemented approval controls. A lender covenant increases pressure to overstate earnings. The team initially planned interim testing before the ERP conversion. Illustrative risk inputs: For one assertion, acceptable audit risk is 3%, inherent risk is 60%, and control risk is 50%. These percentages are a teaching illustration, not a prescribed audit formula for every engagement. Required: Risk associated with ineffective approval controls.

choices.text: Control risk
Detection risk
Only sampling risk
No financial-reporting implication

questions.explanation: Relevant controls may fail to prevent or detect errors.

questions.topic: Understand the Entity & Design the Audit Strategy
questions.prompt: A distributor is entering a new market and implementing a new ERP. Match each issue to the appropriate audit concept or response. Planning observations: Complex warranty estimates require substantial judgment. The new ERP has not implemented approval controls. A lender covenant increases pressure to overstate earnings. The team initially planned interim testing before the ERP conversion. Illustrative risk inputs: For one assertion, acceptable audit risk is 3%, inherent risk is 60%, and control risk is 50%. These percentages are a teaching illustration, not a prescribed audit formula for every engagement. Required: Illustrative detection risk, as a percentage.

questions.topic: Understand the Entity & Design the Audit Strategy
questions.prompt: A distributor is entering a new market and implementing a new ERP. Match each issue to the appropriate audit concept or response. Planning observations: Complex warranty estimates require substantial judgment. The new ERP has not implemented approval controls. A lender covenant increases pressure to overstate earnings. The team initially planned interim testing before the ERP conversion. Illustrative risk inputs: For one assertion, acceptable audit risk is 3%, inherent risk is 60%, and control risk is 50%. These percentages are a teaching illustration, not a prescribed audit formula for every engagement. Required: Response to post-conversion risks.

choices.text: Rely entirely on pre-conversion work
Assume the ERP improves every control
Reassess timing and add appropriate post-conversion procedures
Reduce evidence because management is busy

questions.explanation: Evidence from the old system may not address risks in the new system.

questions.topic: Internal Controls, Walkthroughs & Service Organizations
questions.prompt: Which COSO component includes the tone at the top and commitment to integrity?

choices.text: Control activities only.
Detection risk.
Control environment.
Substantive procedures.

questions.explanation: The control environment provides the foundation for the other internal-control components.

questions.topic: Internal Controls, Walkthroughs & Service Organizations
questions.prompt: An auditor follows one transaction through a process and inspects evidence of approval. What does this most directly support?

choices.text: A conclusion that every approval operated throughout the year.
A guarantee that fraud is impossible.
A direct opinion on every IT system.
Understanding design and implementation.

questions.explanation: A walkthrough helps understand the process and implementation. Period-long operating effectiveness requires appropriate additional evidence.

questions.topic: Internal Controls, Walkthroughs & Service Organizations
questions.prompt: Which combination creates the clearest segregation-of-duties concern?

choices.text: One employee maintains vendor records, approves payments, and reconciles the bank.
One employee enters invoices and another approves payments.
A custodian is separate from the ledger accountant.
An independent reviewer investigates bank reconciling items.

questions.explanation: Combining authorization, record control, and reconciliation enables errors or fraud to be initiated and concealed.

questions.topic: Internal Controls, Walkthroughs & Service Organizations
questions.prompt: Which service-auditor report is generally most relevant to operating effectiveness of outsourced payroll controls affecting financial reporting?

choices.text: SOC 1 Type 1 alone.
SOC 1 Type 2.
A general marketing brochure.
An unrelated SOC 2 confidentiality report alone.

questions.explanation: SOC 1 addresses financial-reporting controls, and Type 2 adds operating-effectiveness testing over a period.

questions.topic: Internal Controls, Walkthroughs & Service Organizations
questions.prompt: A SOC report identifies user controls that the client has not implemented. What should the auditor do?

choices.text: Ignore them because the provider has an unmodified report.
Assume the service auditor tested the client’s controls.
Evaluate the missing controls and adjust the audit response.
Remove payroll from the audit scope.

questions.explanation: Complementary user-entity controls are part of the assumed control system and may require testing or a changed substantive response.

questions.topic: Internal Controls, Walkthroughs & Service Organizations
questions.prompt: Why are change-management controls relevant to an automated three-way matching control?

choices.text: Automated controls never depend on IT general controls.
Change controls establish ownership of inventory.
They replace all invoice evidence.
Unauthorized program changes could alter how the matching control operates.

questions.explanation: Relevant IT general controls support continued reliable operation of automated application controls.

questions.topic: Internal Controls, Walkthroughs & Service Organizations
questions.prompt: Evaluate the design and evidence of controls in an order-to-cash cycle. Process narrative: Sales staff can create customers and approve their own credit limits. Shipments are entered through a system with a documented matching control. Developers can alter that control directly in production. The outsourced billing provider supplied only a SOC 1 Type 1 report. Audit objective: The team wants to rely on relevant controls throughout the year. A single observed transaction matched successfully. No testing over the period has been performed. Required: Concern in customer and credit approval.

choices.text: Incompatible authorization responsibilities
A complete independent credit review
Only a presentation issue
No control risk

questions.explanation: Self-approval weakens independent authorization.

questions.topic: Internal Controls, Walkthroughs & Service Organizations
questions.prompt: Evaluate the design and evidence of controls in an order-to-cash cycle. Process narrative: Sales staff can create customers and approve their own credit limits. Shipments are entered through a system with a documented matching control. Developers can alter that control directly in production. The outsourced billing provider supplied only a SOC 1 Type 1 report. Audit objective: The team wants to rely on relevant controls throughout the year. A single observed transaction matched successfully. No testing over the period has been performed. Required: Concern in production program access.

choices.text: Guaranteed operating effectiveness
Unauthorized change risk
A physical inventory issue only
A sufficient compensating control

questions.explanation: Developers could bypass authorized and tested changes.

questions.topic: Internal Controls, Walkthroughs & Service Organizations
questions.prompt: Evaluate the design and evidence of controls in an order-to-cash cycle. Process narrative: Sales staff can create customers and approve their own credit limits. Shipments are entered through a system with a documented matching control. Developers can alter that control directly in production. The outsourced billing provider supplied only a SOC 1 Type 1 report. Audit objective: The team wants to rely on relevant controls throughout the year. A single observed transaction matched successfully. No testing over the period has been performed. Required: What the Type 1 report does not establish.

choices.text: The report’s date
The report’s stated scope
Operating effectiveness over the period
The system description included

questions.explanation: Type 1 is an at-a-date design report.

questions.topic: Internal Controls, Walkthroughs & Service Organizations
questions.prompt: Evaluate the design and evidence of controls in an order-to-cash cycle. Process narrative: Sales staff can create customers and approve their own credit limits. Shipments are entered through a system with a documented matching control. Developers can alter that control directly in production. The outsourced billing provider supplied only a SOC 1 Type 1 report. Audit objective: The team wants to rely on relevant controls throughout the year. A single observed transaction matched successfully. No testing over the period has been performed. Required: Additional evidence for planned reliance.

choices.text: Only the original inquiry
A client waiver
No work after one successful match
Appropriate tests of operating effectiveness

questions.explanation: Planned reliance requires evidence across the relevant period.

questions.topic: Materiality, Fraud & Planned Responses
questions.prompt: A case specifies overall materiality as 4% of $3,000,000 pretax income and performance materiality as 75% of overall materiality. What is performance materiality?
questions.explanation: Overall materiality is $120,000; 75% is $90,000. The case supplies the percentages rather than prescribing universal audit rules.

questions.topic: Materiality, Fraud & Planned Responses
questions.prompt: A $10,000 deliberate misstatement causes an entity to meet a loan covenant. It is below the audit’s numerical materiality benchmark. What is appropriate?

choices.text: Consider its qualitative significance and intentional nature.
Automatically disregard it.
Treat it as clearly trivial without evaluation.
Conclude all covenants are irrelevant to financial reporting.

questions.explanation: Nature and circumstances can make a quantitatively small item material to users.

questions.topic: Materiality, Fraud & Planned Responses
questions.prompt: Why is performance materiality ordinarily lower than overall materiality?

choices.text: To guarantee all errors are found.
To address the risk of aggregate undetected and uncorrected misstatements.
To eliminate sampling risk.
To set the maximum client fee.

questions.explanation: A margin below overall materiality reduces aggregation risk; it does not guarantee detection.

questions.topic: Materiality, Fraud & Planned Responses
questions.prompt: Three uncorrected misstatements affect income in the same direction by $40,000, $35,000, and $30,000. Overall materiality is $100,000. What is their aggregate effect?

choices.text: Only $40,000 because it is the largest.
$5,000 because only the excess is a misstatement.
$105,000, requiring aggregate evaluation.
Zero because every individual item is below materiality.

questions.explanation: All three items are accumulated: 40,000 + 35,000 + 30,000 = 105,000.

questions.topic: Materiality, Fraud & Planned Responses
questions.prompt: Management corrects a fraudulent top-side entry identified by the auditor. What remains necessary?

choices.text: Ignore it because the balance is now correct.
Automatically issue an unmodified opinion without other work.
Delete the evidence of the original entry.
Evaluate implications for other misstatements, control reliability, and management integrity.

questions.explanation: Correction resolves the identified amount but not the broader implications of intentional misstatement.

questions.topic: Materiality, Fraud & Planned Responses
questions.prompt: Which audit risk requires attention even when normal transaction controls seem strong?

choices.text: Management override.
Only the risk of an invoice being printed late.
Only the risk of an audit fee being unpaid.
No risk remains after controls are documented.

questions.explanation: Management can bypass controls that otherwise operate effectively, requiring targeted responses.

questions.topic: Materiality, Fraud & Planned Responses
questions.prompt: Prepare a materiality worksheet and evaluate an uncorrected-adjustment schedule. Planning policy for this case: Pretax income: $4,000,000. Overall materiality: 5% of pretax income. Performance materiality: 65% of overall materiality. The policy is supplied for this exercise. Uncorrected expense understatements: Accrual A: $90,000. Accrual B: $70,000. Accrual C: $55,000. An additional deliberate $8,000 adjustment changes a covenant outcome. Required: Overall materiality.

questions.prompt: Prepare a materiality worksheet and evaluate an uncorrected-adjustment schedule. Planning policy for this case: Pretax income: $4,000,000. Overall materiality: 5% of pretax income. questions.topic: Materiality, Fraud & Planned Responses
questions.prompt: Prepare a materiality worksheet and evaluate an uncorrected-adjustment schedule. Planning policy for this case: Pretax income: $4,000,000. Overall materiality: 5% of pretax income. Performance materiality: 65% of overall materiality. The policy is supplied for this exercise. Uncorrected expense understatements: Accrual A: $90,000. Accrual B: $70,000. Accrual C: $55,000. An additional deliberate $8,000 adjustment changes a covenant outcome. Required: Treatment of the covenant adjustment.

choices.text: Evaluate qualitative significance despite its size
Ignore it solely because it is small
Automatically exclude deliberate entries
Treat it as an audit fee

questions.explanation: Intent and covenant effects can be qualitatively material.

questions.topic: Specialists, Related Parties & Specialized Engagement Risks
questions.prompt: Management provides a valuation prepared by an expert who has a material financial interest in the client. What should the auditor evaluate?

choices.text: The expert’s objectivity and the relevance and reliability of the work.
Only whether the expert’s report has a professional logo.
Only the number of pages in the report.
Nothing because expertise transfers audit responsibility.

questions.explanation: A financial interest can affect objectivity. The auditor retains responsibility and must evaluate the evidence.

questions.topic: Specialists, Related Parties & Specialized Engagement Risks
questions.prompt: A related-party transaction is labeled arm’s length in a management memo. What is required?

choices.text: Automatic acceptance of the label.
Evidence supporting the transaction’s terms, purpose, and appropriate reporting.
Automatic classification as illegal.
Exclusion from the audit because it is internal.

questions.explanation: Labels do not establish substance. Related-party transactions require appropriate evidence and disclosure evaluation.

questions.topic: Specialists, Related Parties & Specialized Engagement Risks
questions.prompt: Which consideration is relevant before using work of the internal audit function?

choices.text: Whether internal audit can sign the external opinion instead.
Whether the client pays internal audit more than external audit.
Objectivity, competence, and a systematic and disciplined approach.
Whether every internal auditor is a shareholder.

questions.explanation: Evaluate the function and the proposed work; the external auditor’s responsibility remains.

questions.topic: Specialists, Related Parties & Specialized Engagement Risks
questions.prompt: What additional focus is central to a single audit of an entity receiving federal awards?

choices.text: Only the entity’s stock price.
Only its income-tax return.
A guarantee that all grants will be renewed.
Applicable federal-program compliance and major-program requirements.

questions.explanation: Single audits include requirements related to federal awards and compliance under the applicable Uniform Guidance.

questions.topic: Specialists, Related Parties & Specialized Engagement Risks
questions.prompt: An audit of an ERISA employee benefit plan should include attention to which evidence?

choices.text: Plan provisions and participant data relevant to contributions and benefits.
Only the sponsor’s marketing brochure.
Only the sponsor’s projected sales.
Only the auditor’s retirement preference.

questions.explanation: Plan documents and participant information drive important obligations and transactions.

questions.topic: Specialists, Related Parties & Specialized Engagement Risks
questions.prompt: A law directly determines a material liability in the financial statements. Which response is appropriate?

choices.text: Ignore the law because the auditor is not a lawyer.
Obtain evidence about compliance relevant to the material amount.
Assume every law has exactly the same financial-statement effect.
Replace the liability test with an independence letter.

questions.explanation: The auditor’s responsibilities differ by the law’s effect; direct effects on material amounts require appropriate evidence.

questions.topic: Specialists, Related Parties & Specialized Engagement Risks
questions.prompt: Identify an appropriate planning response to each engagement fact. Engagement observations: A valuation is prepared by a financially interested management specialist. A CEO-controlled company supplies a material loan. A public charity expends federal awards subject to a single audit. A pension plan’s participant eligibility records are incomplete. Planning limits: The exercise asks for audit responses, not a legal conclusion or an official program threshold. Assume the described specialized engagement requirements apply. Required: Response to the specialist interest.

choices.text: Accept credentials as sufficient
Transfer the audit opinion to the specialist
Evaluate objectivity and corroborate the valuation evidence
Ignore material estimates

questions.explanation: Objectivity and evidential quality need assessment.

questions.prompt: Identify an appropriate planning response to each engagement fact. Engagement observations: A valuation is prepared by a financially interested management specialist. A CEO-controlled company supplies a material loan. A public charity expends federal awards subject to a single audit. A pension plan’s participant eligibility records are incomplete. Planning limits: The exercise asks for audit responses, not a legal conclusion or an official program threshold. Assume the described specialized engagement requirements apply. Required: Response to the CEO-controlled lender.

choices.text: Assume arm’s length
Ignore the loan
Automatically conclude the loan is illegal
Investigate related-party terms and disclosure

questions.explanation: Establish substance and appropriate disclosure.

Required: Additional focus for the charity.

choices.text: Federal-award compliance and major-program work
Only common-stock valuation
Only product warranties
No additional requirements

questions.explanation: Single audits add compliance and program requirements.

questions.prompt: Identify an appropriate planning response to each engagement fact. Engagement observations: A valuation is prepared by a financially interested management specialist. A CEO-controlled company supplies a material loan. A public charity expends federal awards subject to a single audit. A pension plan’s participant eligibility records are incomplete. Planning limits: The exercise asks for audit responses, not a legal conclusion or an official program threshold. Assume the described specialized engagement requirements apply. Required: Response to missing plan eligibility data.

Obtain reliable support for affected participant and benefit information
Ignore plan provisions

questions.explanation: Participant data is important evidence in the plan audit.
